Below is description of the three pathways: 

Pathway  CP1 [High Flex]  CP2 [High dispatch]  CP3 [High Renewables] 

Pathway description 

Fast development of renewables alongside the highest level of energy storage capacity and consumer engagement in demand flexibility. Minimal new dispatchable low carbon power. 

Growth in renewables but the lowest of all pathways. Highest deployment of low carbon dispatchable power alongside highest nuclear capacity. 

Highest level of renewables capacity across all pathways. Growth in flexibility in line with CP2 (High Dispatch) and minimal dispatchable low carbon power in line with CP1 (High Flex). 

Demand assumptions [...] consumers, community impacts, energy security, how the pathways support decarbonisation beyond the power sector and the wider journey to net zero beyond 2030, wider impacts on the economy and environment. 

Our analysis will consider the actions that government, Ofgem, NESO and industry could take to deliver on the clean power mission across five critical enablers we have so far identified which are: 

• Planning, consenting and communities 

• Grid connections reform 

• Markets, funding and financing 

• Supply chains and workforce 

• Institutions and governance

Transport, heat and industry electrification is driven by the requirement to meet overall emission reduction targets in 2030s. Energy efficiency improvements grow. Highest engagement with residential and industrial DSR, other demand flexibility sectors aligned to other pathways.

tavily_results.title: Coal to clean – the UK's decarbonisation story | National Energy System Operator
tavily_results.content:
We are working with the Powering Past Coal Alliance, GO15 and the newly formed Global Power System Transformation Consortium to do just that. Through these international organisations we can share our knowledge and expertise with system operators, regulators, legislators, and policy makers across the world, helping each other on our decarbonisation journey.

We’ve proved that you can take an energy system with little renewable generation and transform it into a cleaner and greener system with deliverable plans for zero carbon operation.

I look forward to sharing more of this with you over the coming year. [...] Our journey from coal to clean rapidly accelerated in 1992. That was the year that new legislation allowed the use of gas to generate electricity. Of course, gas is by no means a clean fuel, but the carbon output is substantially lower than coal.

The ‘Dash for Gas’ of the early 1990s transformed the industry, bringing more competition and a focus on consumers. By the early 2000s, gas power peaked, and new priorities emerged. The UK set itself ambitious decarbonisation targets, and the renewables revolution began.

> Undertaking such a transformation makes you think more about the future. And the switch to gas prompted us to look at the network requirements for the next several decades. [...] This variability of renewables means that we need robust operability plans to ensure they can be utilised when they are available, and we have alternatives when they are not.

We’ve achieved this by developing new services, provided by both fossil fuel and renewable generators. These services support the network, enabling it to adapt to fluctuations in supply from renewables.

Today our greatest challenge is shifting the provision of these services from fossil fuel generators to renewable sources – many have doubted that this could be done.

local_documents.snippet: Environmental Burden of Disease from Coal-Fired Power Plants in Germany Environmental Burden of Disease from Coal-Fired Power Plants in Germany This study estimates the health burden in Germany caused by long-term exposure to nitrogen dioxide and PM2.5 emissions from hard coal- and lignite-fired power plants in 2015. The authors focus on source-specific disease burden rather than total air pollution, asking how much disease could be attributed specifically to emissions from these coal power plants. The central conclusion is that both hard coal and lignite contributed a measurable burden of disease, with lignite producing the larger impact for both pollutants. The methodology combines air pollution modeling, population exposure assessment, and health burden calculation. local_documents.snippet: to Ambient PM2.5 Mortality This paper provides a global assessment of which sectors and fuels contribute most to ambient PM2.5 exposure and PM2.5-attributable mortality. The motivation is practical: fine particulate matter is the world's leading environmental health risk, but effective air quality policy requires knowing which sources drive the burden in different places. The study covers 21 world regions, 204 countries, and 200 sub-national areas, allowing comparison across global, national, and urban-relevant scales. The methodology combines atmospheric modeling, satellite-based exposure estimates, emissions inventories, and disease-specific health risk functions. The authors ran 24 sensitivity simulations with the GEOS-Chem global chemical transport model to estimate source and fuel contributions. local_documents.snippet: to reduce air pollution from all major sources, improve public health, protect the natural environment, and support cleaner economic growth. It begins from the position that the country has already reduced many of the worst pollution problems through regulation, industrial investment, and a cleaner energy mix, but that air pollution remains one of the UK's largest public health challenges. The strategy stresses that harmful emissions now come from many diffuse sources, not only from large factories or road traffic. The document identifies air pollution as a result of how the UK generates power, heats homes, produces food, manufactures goods, and moves people and freight. It focuses on five damaging pollutants covered by legally binding international reduction commitments: fine particulate matter, ammonia, nitrogen oxides, sulphur dioxide, and non-methane volatile organic compounds. local_documents.snippet: ticles are recognized as important concerns, but the evidence was not sufficient to derive full quantitative air quality guideline values. WHO recommends monitoring, exposure assessment, source control where possible, and risk communication for these particle types. Implementation is presented as a policy process, not just a measurement exercise. Countries are encouraged to assess national needs and capacity, translate the guideline levels into enforceable standards where appropriate, build air quality management systems, and use health risk assessment to compare policy options. WHO stresses the role of the health sector in synthesizing evidence, communicating risks, monitoring impacts, and supporting decision-making, while also making clear that air pollution control requires cooperation across transport, energy, housing, industry, agriculture, urban planning, and environmental agencies
